GRU4Rec’s original follow-up identifies an objective bottleneck: averaging BPR over many easy negatives dilutes useful gradients. BPR-max instead minimizes −log Σⱼ softmax(s⁻)ⱼ·sigmoid(s⁺−sⱼ⁻), with negative-score regularization, emphasizing competitive negatives. The maintained implementation recommends BPR-max or cross-entropy and supports sampling proportional to frequency^α, interpolating uniform and popularity sampling. These provide direct loss/sampler ablations without changing GRU memory. [Original paper](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf), [implementation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec). A 2024 sequential-recommendation study finds uniform sampling favors head items, while popularity/in-batch sampling can improve balance at an overall accuracy cost; its backbone is SASRec, so transfer to GRU4Rec remains a hypothesis. [Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276).

Harder is not always better. WWW 2026’s R²NS reports failures from introducing hard negatives too early; uniform warm-up followed by progressively harder stochastic selection improves training, while sampling among top-ranked candidates reduces deterministic hardest-negative selection’s false-negative risk. [R²NS](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf). RecSys 2025 also revisits sampled-softmax logQ correction: the positive is always included, unlike sampled negatives, requiring distinct treatment. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331). Practical hypotheses: separately test regularized BPR-max, multi-negative sampled softmax, and warm-up plus stochastic hard-negative sampling; hold retention initialization fixed. Exclude padding, target collisions and observed training positives from negatives, without consulting held-out labels. The supplied 14.49% versus 2.86% gap motivates these experiments but does not establish their cause. Track frequency-stratified diagnostics while selecting exclusively by fixed macro validation HR@10, retaining one jointly trained GRU4Rec per category.
